name: Micah

timeline.note: Micah 1:1 dates his ministry across the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, roughly the mid-to-late 700s BC, but gives no personal birth or death year, so no specific date is plotted.

source_summary: Contemporary of Isaiah who confronted corrupt rulers and empty religion, famous for predicting the Messiah's birth in Bethlehem and summarizing true religion as doing justice, loving kindness, and walking humbly with God.
family_friendly_summary: Micah was a prophet from a small town in Judah who spoke out against unfair rulers and prophets who only cared about money, at the same time that Isaiah was prophesying nearby. Micah warned that Jerusalem would face serious trouble if people didn't change their ways — and years later, this warning was remembered as an example of a true prophet being taken seriously instead of punished. Micah is most famous for two things: he predicted that a great ruler would be born in the small town of Bethlehem, which came true when Jesus was born there. He also gave one of the Bible's best summaries of what God wants from us: to act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with God. Micah's story shows that following God isn't about religious show — it's about how we actually treat others.
adult_story: Micah, from the town of Moresheth in Judah, prophesied during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, contemporary with Isaiah, and confronted the same corruption Amos had denounced in the north — corrupt rulers, false prophets who prophesied for money, and a people who thought God's presence guaranteed their safety (Micah 1:1; 3:1-12). His warning that Jerusalem would become "a heap of ruins" was serious enough that, decades later, Hezekiah's fear of the LORD in response to it was cited in Jeremiah's own defense at his trial, as proof a true prophet's hard word could be received rather than punished (Jeremiah 26:18-19). Micah is best known for two passages reaching far beyond his own day: his prophecy that a ruler over Israel would come from the small town of Bethlehem, "whose origin is from of old, from ancient days" (Micah 5:2), which the chief priests and scribes quoted to Herod as the Messiah's birthplace (Matthew 2:5-6); and his summary of what true religion requires — not endless sacrifices, but "to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God" (Micah 6:6-8). Micah's book closes in confident hope in God's compassion, who "will again have compassion on us" and cast Israel's sins into the depths of the sea (Micah 7:18-19).
